elements.label: Hotter, drier summers
elements.description: Meteorological drought (KNMI'23): higher evaporation, summer precipitation deficit, and lower river discharge.

elements.label: Sea-level rise
elements.description: Rising sea level (KNMI'23 scenarios); increases hydrostatic pressure of marine water on polders and estuaries.

elements.label: Wetter winters
elements.description: Increased winter precipitation, providing potential recharge volume if retained.

elements.label: Crop water demand
elements.description: The water the crops use in the growing season when they have enough, whatever its origin: the crop's evapotranspiration, set by the weather (radiation, air temperature, humidity and wind speed) and by the crop and its stage of growth (Allen et al., 1998, FAO-56, a guide to crop water use that holds wherever the crop grows). It follows the weather within the season, highest in sunny, warm and dry weather: an Auxiliary.

elements.label: Estuary salt intrusion
elements.description: Marine water penetrating further inland into estuaries and surface canals when sea levels rise and river discharge drops.

elements.label: Freshwater lens recharge
elements.description: The rain that soaks in and refills the rainwater lens: mostly the winter's rain surplus, since in summer most of the rain evaporates (van Beekom et al., 1953a, for the Netherlands). On Schouwen-Duiveland it soaks deep into the dunes and the sandy creek ridges, while in the low polders upward saline seepage keeps it within the clay top layer and tile drains carry much of it off during each rain; recharge, seepage and drainage depth together set the lens's thickness (de Louw et al., 2011, measured on the island).

elements.label: Freshwater lens thickness
elements.description: The thickness of the fresh rainwater lens on top of the saline groundwater, from the surface to the middle of the mixing zone between them. On Schouwen-Duiveland it is about 2 m on average in the low-lying polders with saline seepage, under 2 m over more than half of the 56 km² surveyed, and 5 to 15 m under the sandy creek ridges (de Louw et al., 2011, measured on the island from a helicopter and on the ground); lenses reach about 30 m under the creek ridges and the dunes, and nearly 100 m under the dunes (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10). A Stock: a year's recharge barely moves it (Freshwater lens recharge → Freshwater lens thickness).

elements.label: Land subsidence
elements.description: Peat oxidation and clay consolidation caused by low drainage levels, lowering the land surface relative to sea level.

elements.label: Polder surface elevation (NAP)
elements.description: Physical land surface elevation of the polder (-1.5m to -3.5m NAP), lowered by subsidence. Tidal silt, let in through a wisselpolder, would barely raise it on this island: the Grevelingen has no tide, and the Oosterschelde has too little silt to raise polders on a large scale (De Mesel et al., 2013). Since the storm surge barrier its channels carry 52–70% less suspended sediment (Ma et al., 2014), under 10 mg/l near Zierikzee, and its salt marshes rise 3–10 mm a year (van Maldegem & de Jong, 2004), against 16–32 mm on young marshes along the Westerschelde (De Mesel et al., 2013).

elements.label: Root zone salinity
elements.description: The salt concentration of the soil water in the crop root zone. Salt harms a crop in two phases: at once osmotically, slowing the growth of young leaves, and more slowly as sodium (Na+) or chloride (Cl-) builds up in the leaves, ageing the older ones early (Munns & Tester, 2008, a review of plant physiology, which holds wherever the crop grows). It rises in a dry summer as the soil dries out and salt rises by capillary rise, and falls with the winter's rain surplus, which washes the topsoil of well-drained soil free of salt in one winter and that of badly drained soil in two or three (van Beekom et al., 1953a, measured after the floods in Zeeland): within the year where the soil drains well, so an Auxiliary.

elements.label: Saline seepage (kwel)
elements.description: The upward flow of salt groundwater from the sand below into the clay and peat top layer of the island's polders, in mm a day, which leaves through drains, ditches and evaporation (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3662). The higher water pressure at depth drives it in the low polders, where it keeps the rainwater lenses thin, mostly under 2 m, and the shallow groundwater brackish to salt (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10); below the lens its water holds 10 to 16 g of chloride a litre (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3675), against about 16 to 17 g in North Sea water (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10). Most of Duiveland gets salt seepage, most in its low parts near the Oosterschelde (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 27); in the western low polders it is strongest near the Grevelingen and the Oosterschelde (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 27). The flow follows the water pressures, which change constantly with recharge and drainage (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3675): within the year, so an Auxiliary.

elements.label: Soil structure
elements.description: The soil's aggregates and pores, which set how fast water soaks in: well-drained clay with its structure intact let the winter's rain surplus soak through almost completely, while clay whose structure sodium had broken down became impervious and sticky when wet (van Beekom et al., 1953a, 1953b, measured after the floods in Zeeland). A Stock: once broken down, it recovers over years (Root zone salinity → Soil structure). Workability, which structure and wetness both shape, is Spring workability of the fields.

elements.label: Upconing of salt groundwater
elements.description: Upward cone of the salt-freshwater interface beneath pumping irrigation wells as the freshwater lens thins.

elements.label: Brackish irrigation water use
elements.description: Irrigation with salinised surface or well water, when fresh water falls short.

elements.label: Farmers' demand for deep polder drainage
elements.description: Farmers' wish for low ditch levels, so that their fields drain: dry enough in spring for heavy machinery to work them, which holding water back for dry times makes hard (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021c, p. 44), and free of water damage after heavy rain, which farmers in the island's western low polders often find a bigger problem than drought (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 27). They put it to the water board as it prepares its water level plans, which it does with interest groups such as farming, and in views on a draft (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 17): on Duiveland's draft of 2021, four views feared that a raise the plan proposed to study would bring more flooding in extreme rain (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 53). Within the year, so an Auxiliary.

elements.label: Fresh water supplied to the island
elements.description: Fresh water brought to the island's farms from outside it in the growing season (present in Tholen and Zeeuws-Vlaanderen; absent on Walcheren, the Bevelanden and Schouwen-Duiveland). It needs a supply route, and in drought it is what the national distribution leaves for the route to carry.

elements.label: Freshwater availability for crops
elements.description: Fresh water crops can draw on in the growing season: rain, the soil moisture and groundwater of the field above the lens, water farmers pump or have stored, and water supplied from outside, which reaches the island nowhere now (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 4, 8). It follows the weather within the season: an Auxiliary.

elements.label: Freshwater storage measures
elements.description: The fresh water a year that the measures in place on the island's farms keep, store or collect for the growing season. They work three ways (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 16–23, 53, for the island): in the low polders, controlled drainage, anti-salinisation drainage (Drains2Buffer) and weirs in ditches keep the thin rainwater lens against salt, the water staying in the field's own soil, where it cannot be pumped (pp. 33, 53); on the creek ridges, the dunes and where a sand layer lies under the clay, the creek-ridge infiltration system, the Freshmaker and underground storage under a clay layer infiltrate winter water to pump in summer (pp. 20–22, 38); and double drainage collects fresh drain water into a basin to irrigate from (pp. 23, 29, 32). An adaptive practice: measures to keep more fresh water in the ground as drought and salinisation increase (p. 4). The study found them not yet fitted to the island and too risky for many farms to invest in alone (pp. 4, 11). A Stock: a measure, once built, lasts 15 to 30 years (pp. 17–22, 34). The farm decides a measure; infiltrating water needs the water board's permit or a notification, a weir the neighbours' consent, and raising a ditch's level the water board's cooperation (pp. 26, 44–45). Whether a farm wants to store weighs storing against its other ways through a dry summer (pumping, brackish water, other crops), where capacity to invest is whether it can. Stored water pays back over years, which suits a farm that owns its land more than one on a short lease; and where stored water spreads under the neighbours, one farm pays and others gain. Whether either holds a farm back is a question for the group model building session.
elements.simplification: Three ways in one element: keeping the low polders' rainwater lens, infiltrating winter water to pump on the creek ridges and the dunes, and collecting drain water in a basin, counted together as the fresh water they keep, store or collect. Each way adds fresh water and none takes it away, so the sum keeps the sign of every link into and out of it, and where a link works through one way only, its description says which. What one element leaves out: the ways work in different places, through different routes and under different permits and consent, which the description names. Arable land farmed by its owner, a Constant that made storing more worthwhile, is in the description instead: no loop runs through a Constant, so none changes, and the share cannot be set as an input of its own.

elements.label: Groundwater extraction for irrigation
elements.description: Fresh water farmers pump from the fresh groundwater through their own wells, to irrigate or to flush their fields in summer; the water board's pumping stations belong to drainage. The water board sets the rules: a horizontal well at most 6 m below the surface and 80 to 200 m long, at least 200 m from the next well and 50 m from a neighbour's field, pumping at most 800 m³ per hectare and 8,000 m³ per well a year (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b); in Zeeland only from fresh groundwater more than 15 m thick, outside vulnerable areas (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 26). Whose lens a well draws on, the farm's own or one it shares with its neighbours, so that a farm pumping less leaves water to them, is a hypothesis for the group model building session; the rules are written so that a well's effects stay within the farm's own field (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021), an aim of the rules rather than a measurement. Pumping follows the season's shortfall within the year: an Auxiliary.

elements.label: Objections to land-use plans
elements.description: Objections, appeals at the Council of State (Raad van State) and political pressure against plans for the island's water and land, the water board's water level plans among them, which slow, change or stop a plan.

elements.label: Winter rain drained away
elements.description: Winter precipitation rapidly discharged to sea via field drains and pumping stations instead of recharging the lens.

elements.label: Crop yield
elements.description: Physical yield per hectare of conventional crops (potatoes, onions, sugar beet) under the prevailing freshwater, soil and workability conditions; what salt takes from their harvest is Harvest lost to salt. The island's arable farms grow potatoes, onions, sugar beet, cereals, grass seed and vegetables in rotation (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 30, 38, from the farms studied), and some in the low polders have stopped growing sown onions for the salt (p. 31). A season's harvest: an Auxiliary.
elements.simplification: The current crops (potatoes, onions, sugar beet) are one yield per hectare. Each yields less with a larger water shortfall, worse soil structure or fields that cannot be worked in time, so every link into the yield keeps its sign for each crop and no loop through it changes. What one yield leaves out: the crops lose in different proportions (the yield response factors on Crop water shortfall → Crop yield), and farms can shift their rotation among them, as some in the low polders stopped growing sown onions for the salt.

elements.label: Market demand for alternative crops
elements.description: Consumer demand and offtake contracts for novel salt-tolerant or alternative crops (e.g. protein crops).

elements.label: Local processing capacity for new crops
elements.description: Plants and supply chains on or near the island that store, process or sell new salt-tolerant crops. Breeding of tolerant varieties is Salt-tolerant varieties on offer. Buyers and processors build or keep it where they find it worthwhile against processing the crops elsewhere.

elements.label: Adoption of new salt-tolerant crops
elements.description: Hectares under crops new to the island's rotations that tolerate salt (quinoa, samphire, sea aster), which need other machines, knowledge and buyers than the current crops. Farmers grow one where they find it worthwhile against their current crops; capacity to invest is whether they can, and dependence on the current crops what holds them.

elements.label: Agricultural land value
elements.description: The price farmland sells for (€/ha), set by what buyers expect it to earn; banks value it as collateral in their own risk assessment.

elements.label: Risk premium on farm loans
elements.description: The interest banks charge arable farms above their own funding cost, for the risk they see in the loan.

elements.label: Basel IV capital requirements
elements.description: European banking regulations requiring stricter risk weighting on loans when climate/soil risks reduce collateral value.

elements.label: Dependence on high-margin salt-sensitive crops
elements.description: The share of high-value, salt-sensitive cash crops (seed potatoes, onions) in the rotation, which a farm with high debt payments needs to keep up its income, and which the machines and know-how it would lose by switching tie it to.

elements.label: Farm income
elements.description: Farms' revenue from crop sales, set by yield and prices, minus their costs (the water board's levy, interest, their own pumping), per hectare in a year.

elements.label: Farmers' capacity to invest
elements.description: What a farm has left to invest after its debt payments and rent, beside the credit a bank will give it.

elements.label: Owners' concern about their land's value
elements.description: Landowning farmers' concern that their land loses value, from a fall that has happened or from a plan that would lower it. A tenant's concern, losing the lease, is not part of it.

elements.label: Financial leverage
elements.description: The farm's debt relative to the value of its assets, the inverse of its solvency (equity as a share of total capital). Land is 70% of an arable farm's balance sheet, so the ratio moves with the land price: arable farms' solvency was 81% in 2018 because their land had risen in value, while their long-term debt had tripled since 2001 to 770,000 euro per farm (van der Meulen et al., 2020).

elements.label: Arable land in the polders
elements.description: Hectares of the island's land farmed as arable land, with conventional or salt-tolerant crops, whoever owns it. It falls when land that changes hands goes to a holder who does not farm it as arable land; what the land becomes then (nature, grassland, water storage) waits for the group's system boundary.

elements.label: Crop water shortfall
elements.description: What crops need in the growing season beyond the water they get, fresh or brackish: the gap farmers' water decisions respond to. The island's farms depend wholly on rain and on the fresh groundwater under the dunes, the creek ridges and the thin rainwater lenses of the low polders; with no link to the main freshwater system, no fresh water can be brought in and no ditches flushed in dry periods, so the farms run short of water, as the dry years 2018, 2019 and 2020 showed (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 8). It follows the weather within the season: an Auxiliary.

elements.label: Flushing salt from the root zone
elements.description: Fresh water farmers put on a field to wash salt below the roots, pumped from the lens.

elements.label: Freshwater supply route to the island
elements.description: Pipes or channels that could bring fresh water to the island, as their capacity in a summer; none exists. Who decides on one and who pays is on the facts list under External freshwater supply; news reports say the province has costed a pipeline (unread at the source).

elements.label: Spring workability of the fields
elements.description: Whether heavy machinery can work the fields early in spring without damaging the soil, set by soil structure and by how wet the soil is.

elements.label: Polder drainage depth
elements.description: How far below the surface the water board holds the ditch levels in the island's polders (the drooglegging), as its water level plans set them: Duiveland's plan sets a target level for each of its level areas, from 0.8 to 2.7 m below NAP, in most the summer level higher than the winter one, against nature's order, to prevent water damage in winter and drying in summer (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, pp. 37, 63–64). It moves from the winter level to the summer one in steps in March and April, as the weather and the farmers' soil work allow (p. 66). On a creek ridge studied for water storage the depth is over 1.5 m in winter in large parts (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 42). The depth holds until the board carries out a new plan: Duiveland's plan of 2021 replaced one from 1982 (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 24), and the board checks each plan every three years and renews it at 17 years or once it no longer fits (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 16–17), so a Stock. Where the land subsides under a level held, the depth shrinks until a new plan lowers the level, as the board has done where there is peat (2025, p. 13).

elements.label: Water board's plans to raise ditch levels
elements.description: The water level plans in which Waterschap Scheldestromen raises a polder's ditch levels, from the draft until their levels take effect. The board matches its levels to the land's use and soil, its principle that the level follows the land use: arable land 80 to 120 cm below the surface by soil, permanent grassland 20 cm less (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 29; 2025, pp. 5, 7), weighing flooding, drought, fresh water and groundwater (2021c, p. 19), subsidence (2025, pp. 13–14) and a change's costs against its benefits (2025, p. 12). On Duiveland the plan of 2021 proposed studying a raise in 14 level areas, where levels had been kept low to store extreme rain, to enlarge the fresh water in the soil and give crops more moisture (2021a, p. 69). The general board adopts each plan (2025, p. 18); of its 30 members, 26 represent the residents and two the owners of unbuilt land, farmland included, appointed by ZLTO's board (Reglement voor het Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, arts. 6–7). A plan waits years for the works its levels need (Water board's plans to raise ditch levels → Polder drainage depth), so a Stock.
elements.simplification: The two seats on the general board for the owners of unbuilt land, farmland included, were a Constant driving these plans, and are in the description instead: no loop runs through a Constant, so no loop changes. What it leaves out: the seats cannot be set as an input of their own.

elements.label: Water board's pumping costs
elements.description: What Waterschap Scheldestromen spends on its pumping stations to hold the polders' ditch levels: more water to pump the deeper it drains, the more seepage and winter rain come in and the lower the land lies.

elements.label: Water board levy on farmland
elements.description: What the water board charges owners and users of farmland for its water management, pumping included.

elements.label: Harvest lost to salt
elements.description: The conventional crops' harvest that salt in the root zone takes, over the island's fields still under them, in a season. On the island, farms where seepage pressure is high and the surface water is salty all year have stopped growing sensitive crops such as sown onions (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 31). Zeeland is among the coastal provinces where potatoes and barley lose considerable yield to salt (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 12). Salt's effect on yield builds up over weeks to months and is read over the season (Allen et al., 1998, ch. 8): within the year, so an Auxiliary.

elements.label: Margin given up on high-margin crops
elements.description: The margin a farm forgoes on fields it moves from its high-margin current crops to salt-tolerant ones, largest on fresh land, where the current crops still do well.

elements.label: Farms with a successor
elements.description: Arable farms on the island whose farmer has someone to take the farm over.

elements.label: Harvest of new crops to process
elements.description: The volume of new salt-tolerant crops within reach of a processing plant on or near the island, from the island's growers and from growers elsewhere.

elements.label: Net price for new crops after transport
elements.description: What farmers on the island get for new salt-tolerant crops once transport to the processor is paid, set by processors on and off the island.

elements.label: Growers of new crops elsewhere
elements.description: Farmers off the island growing the same new crops, whose harvest a local plant could also process.

elements.label: Processing of new crops elsewhere
elements.description: Plants off the island that buy and process new salt-tolerant crops, which set the price the island's growers can get beside a local plant.

elements.label: Adoption of salt-tolerant varieties
elements.description: Hectares under salt-tolerant varieties of the current crops (potato, onion), which use the same machines, storage and know-how. Farmers grow one where they find it worthwhile against the variety they grow now.

elements.label: Salt-tolerant varieties on offer
elements.description: Salt-tolerant varieties of the current crops that breeders bring to market, and their yield; breeding lies outside the CLD's scale.

elements.label: Machines and storage for the current crops
elements.description: The planters, harvesters and stores farms own for their current crops, built up over years and renewed when worn.

elements.label: Capital lost on switching to new crops
elements.description: The machines, storage and know-how a farm writes off when it moves fields to a new crop that cannot use them; what it keeps using or sells is not lost. Salt-tolerant varieties of the current crops lose little of it.

elements.label: Farmers' knowledge of new crops
elements.description: What the island's farmers know about growing and selling new salt-tolerant crops, from their own fields, their neighbours' and advisers.

elements.label: Spending on keeping the current crops
elements.description: What farms invest in carrying on with their current crops: wells and irrigation, drains, new machines and storage.

elements.label: Banks' risk assessment of farm loans
elements.description: The risk a bank sees in lending to an arable farm: its solvency, its collateral at the bank's own valuation, and plans that may change what the land can earn.

elements.label: Bank credit to farms
elements.description: New loans and refinancing that banks grant the island's arable farms.

elements.label: Debt payments
elements.description: Interest and repayments farms owe on their loans in a year.

elements.label: World prices of conventional crops
elements.description: The prices of potatoes, onions and sugar beet on the markets the island's crops are sold on, which its farms cannot move: what carrying on is weighed against.

elements.label: Farmers' trust in government
elements.description: How far the island's farmers expect public bodies to keep their commitments on water and land (compensation, their say over their land).

elements.label: Expropriation of farmland
elements.description: Farmland a public body takes for a public purpose, with compensation, after a legal procedure; which body can do so on the island is on the facts list under Concern about expropriation and devaluation.

elements.label: Farmers' wish to keep their land
elements.description: How strongly farmers hold on to their land beyond its money value: family land, growing up on it. Whether anything on the map moves it, at succession perhaps, is a question for the group model building session.

elements.label: Farmland changing hands
elements.description: Hectares of the island's farmland sold, expropriated or passed on to a new holder in a year: at a forced sale, a retirement without a successor, or otherwise.

elements.label: Farmland planned for other uses
elements.description: Hectares of the island's farmland that Gemeente Schouwen-Duiveland's land-use plan (its omgevingsplan, with the changes it drafts to it) designates for a use other than arable farming, such as nature, water storage, housing or recreation. Which plans the municipality makes for the island's farmland, and where objections enter them, is on the facts list under Objections to land-use plans.

connections.description: Higher temperatures increase evapotranspiration and crop water requirements.
Low summer river discharge allows seawater to penetrate further inland.
Summer precipitation deficit and high evaporation reduce natural recharge.
Rising sea level pushes marine water further into estuaries.
Higher sea level increases hydrostatic pressure beneath dikes.
More winter precipitation increases potential infiltration into the soil.
Higher winter rainfall peaks are mostly discharged under conventional drainage.
Salinisation of surface canals makes intake water for irrigation brackish.

Rainwater infiltration builds up the floating freshwater lens, but slowly: the lens is a stock that a year's recharge barely moves. In the thin polder lenses of Schouwen-Duiveland the mixing zone shifts at most 0.1 m within a year, with vertical flow of at most 1.2 mm per day (de Louw et al., 2011). Under a creek ridge, raising the winter water table 0.5 m thickened a 13–15 m lens by 6–8 m in ten years, and the lens had not reached its new thickness yet (Pauw et al., 2015, a model result for a creek ridge on Walcheren, which transfers since the island's sandy creek ridges also take in rain over saline groundwater: de Louw et al., 2011). On the island's own creek ridge, infiltration with controlled drainage thickened the lens under a 9.5-ha field by up to 3.5 m in ten years (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 44, a groundwater model of 2020–2050). So a change in recharge takes years to a decade to show in the lens.

Where the lens is thin, saline groundwater lies just below the roots and reaches the root zone by capillary rise. In the island's low polders with saline seepage the lens is about 2 m thick, its mixing zone in the clay top layer, and capillary rise of saline groundwater is very likely now, possibly damaging crops (de Louw et al., 2011, measured on Schouwen-Duiveland); the topsoil there is fresh thanks to the rainwater lens, which makes farming possible, and these low polders of heavy clay make up a large part of the island (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 4, 10). Under the creek ridges and the dunes the lens is 5 m thick or more (Freshwater lens thickness), so the link holds in the low polders. Within the year: in a dry season, with the groundwater below the drains, the flow there is only upward (de Louw et al., 2011).
A thicker freshwater lens buffers against salt upconing under wells.

Holds in the low polders, where the thin rainwater lens keeps the topsoil fresh, which makes farming possible there (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10, for the island): water a measure keeps in the lens reaches only the crop on that field, as groundwater and soil moisture, and lies too deep for its roots at germination (p. 33), when most of the island's shortfall falls (pp. 27, 31); later in the summer the soil supplies a well-established crop (p. 27). Under the creek ridges and the dunes the lens is thick, and crops get its water when farms pump it from wells, where it is more than 15 m thick (pp. 26, 38), which is Groundwater extraction for irrigation → Freshwater availability for crops. Within the season.

Peat oxidation and clay settling lower the land surface relative to NAP at millimetres a year, so a decimetre takes decades: Dutch land below sea level is still subsiding up to 1 m per century, fastest in peat areas (Oude Essink et al., 2010). A rate for Schouwen-Duiveland's clay polders is not yet sourced.
Higher polder elevation reduces the hydraulic head difference driving upward saline seepage.

Salt in the root zone puts sodium (Na+) on the clay in place of calcium (Ca2+); once fresh water washes the salt out, clay that holds much sodium disperses: its aggregates and pores collapse, with troubles to be expected above 1 m.e. of exchangeable sodium per 100 g of dry soil. The delay is on the way back: structure collapses within the first winter after the salt leaches out, but the clay only recovers as calcium replaces the sodium again, about 0.7 m.e. Na per 100 g a year, which takes 5 to 10 years on heavy clay and about a year on light soil (van Beekom et al., 1953b, after the 1945 and 1953 floods in Zeeland). Seawater flooding is a much larger salt dose than seepage; soils that took up less sodium recover faster, and no source read shows how much sodium the island's seepage puts on its clay.
connections.simplification: Folds Sodium on the clay, a stock between the two: the salt puts sodium on the clay, and the sodium breaks the clay's structure once the salt washes out. The sign is the product of the two steps (+, then −), so no loop through the link changes, and the stock's slowness is the link's delay. What one link distorts: the delay lies on the way back only, the structure collapsing within the first winter after the salt leaches out and recovering over years, while the link draws one delay for both ways.

connections.description: Upward saline groundwater erodes and thins the floating freshwater lens from below.

Where the rainwater lens over the seepage is thin, salt groundwater reaches the root zone by capillary rise, harming the crops (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3660): in the seepage areas of the island and Zeeland, where the lens's mixing zone lies 1.5 to 2 m below the surface, this is very likely now (p. 3675), and on Duiveland the salt water reaches into or almost into the root zone in places (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 26). Within the year, as the soil dries in summer and the winter's rain washes the salt out (Root zone salinity).

Rain recharges the lens only once it has soaked into the soil. Before the floods, Zeeland's well-drained clay let the winter's rain surplus soak through almost completely; once sodium had broken down the structure of the topsoil, it became impervious and sticky when wet, part of the rain ran off over the surface and pools stood on the land, the more so the heavier the clay (van Beekom et al., 1953a, p. 157; 1953b, p. 233, measured in the flooded polders of Zeeland, by R1's own mechanism). Within the year: the structure a soil has in a winter sets how much of that winter's rain soaks in. Whether what soaks in reaches the lens or leaves through the drains is set by the drainage depth and the seepage (de Louw et al., 2011).
Good soil structure lets roots grow and crops emerge.
Structural soil health and low salinity determine the intrinsic value of arable land.
Salt water drawn upward contaminates the upper soil and irrigation wells.
Evaporation of brackish irrigation water leaves salt behind in the topsoil.
Fresh water supplied from outside adds to what crops can draw on.

Active infiltration adds winter water to the lens, on the creek ridges, the dunes and where a sand layer lies under the clay: the creek-ridge infiltration system raises the groundwater through the drains in winter so the lens grows, and the Freshmaker and underground storage inject winter water through a deep drain or a well, all to pump in summer (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 20–22, 38, for the island). On a creek ridge on the island, infiltration with controlled drainage added about 60,000 m³ of fresh water under a 9.5-ha field in ten years (p. 44, a groundwater model). What limits it on most of the island is fresh water to infiltrate, since the surface water is mostly saline and drain water the likeliest source (pp. 38, 43, 55), and the permit (pp. 26, 45). Within the year: a measure infiltrates from its first winter, and how fast the lens then grows is Freshwater lens recharge → Freshwater lens thickness. The polders' measures keep rain in the field instead, through Winter rain drained away.
Adjustable drains and storage keep winter water in the polder instead of discharging it.

What farmers pump beyond what the rain puts back thins the lens, the boundary with the saline groundwater below rising: the water board's limit of 800 m³ per hectare a year rests on the balance between recharge by rain, irrigation water and extraction, set to keep the fresh groundwater in stock and the fresh-salt boundary from rising (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b), and pumping too fast risks salinisation (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 20–21). Within those rules the effects are meant to stay within the farm's field, with in principle no depletion, and Deltares's modelling of the rules (2018) found them generally enough to prevent strong salinisation under and around the well (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021, for Zeeland). How fast the lens responds to pumping, no source read shows.
Pumping groundwater draws the underlying salt-fresh interface upward into a cone.
Water evacuated via drains cannot infiltrate to refill the freshwater lens.
Higher physical yield increases sales revenue per hectare.

New salt-tolerant crops need less water than the current crops: no source read shows it. FAO-56 (Allen et al., 1998, Tables 11 and 12) lists neither quinoa, samphire nor sea aster, and no source read shows whether the halophytes need less water or take salt water instead.

A fall in the land's value that has happened, through salt in R6: does a farm whose land lost value object harder to the next plan? Through its solvency, yes (−); where compensation pays more than the land would fetch on the market, the concern may fall instead (+). A hypothesis for the group model building session, with both signs as the question to farmers.

With the same mortgage, a lower land value is a higher debt relative to the farm's assets: land is 70% of an arable farm's balance sheet, and its rise in value is what made arable farms' solvency 81% in 2018 (van der Meulen et al., 2020). A high solvency makes new credit easier and cheaper to get; the debt itself does not shrink when the land loses value.
Stricter European banking rules require more capital against climate-exposed loans, which banks price in.

Potatoes and onions are planted and sown in spring, and their soil work must not be done when the soil is too wet, which smears and compacts it and keeps an onion seedbed from forming; a potato crop is best planted early where the soil allows (Verstand et al., 2021, pp. 25, 27, from the Dutch cultivation guides). So the more of the rotation they take, the more farmers need fields that dry early in spring, which holding water back makes hard for farmers who want onto the land with heavy machinery (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021c, p. 44); on Duiveland the board moves to the higher summer level in March and April as the soil work allows (2021a, p. 66). No source read shows how much spring soil work the new crops need: the sign rests on their needing less. Within the year.
High-value salt-sensitive crops require intensive freshwater irrigation during dry spells.
A farm that relies on high margins can give fewer hectares to lower-margin new crops.
Sustained productivity and profitability underpin high market prices for farmland.
Higher farm income generates internal cash flow for adaptive investments.
Capacity to invest decides whether a farm can pay for a storage measure, not whether it wants to.
Capacity to invest decides whether a farm can pay for the switch (new machines, the first years of a new crop), not whether it wants to.
Concern about uncompensated loss leads farmers and their organisations to object, appeal and lobby against such plans.

Once a crop has drawn the root zone down beyond the water it can take up easily, it uses less water than it needs, in proportion to what is left in the root zone (Allen et al., 1998, ch. 8): the shortfall is the part of the demand that rain, soil moisture and irrigation leave unmet, so the more the crops need, the larger it is. On Schouwen-Duiveland's clay a crop that has come up well gets through the summer on the soil's good supply of moisture, so the shortfall falls mostly at germination early in the season, when a small gift of about 20 mm would cover it; onions also need water while they grow (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 27, 31, 38, from talks with the island's farmers). Within the year.

Rain, irrigation and capillary rise from the groundwater add water to the root zone and lower its depletion; once the depletion passes the readily available water, the crop uses less water than it needs (Allen et al., 1998, FAO-56 ch. 8, eqs. 84–85, a daily water balance). So the more fresh water crops can draw on, the smaller the shortfall, within the season. On the island's farms a gift of 20 to 25 mm at germination makes the difference where none can be given now (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 27, 55).

Farmers pump more fresh groundwater as the shortfall grows: the water board registered a considerable increase in extractions in recent years, which the more extreme drought certainly influenced, so the volume pumped rises in dry years (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021, for Zeeland, whose farms pump under the same rules as the island's). On Schouwen-Duiveland the farms get their fresh water from rain and from the fresh groundwater; the shallow groundwater and the ditches are brackish to salt, and no water can be brought in (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 8). They may pump only from fresh groundwater more than 15 m thick, under the creek ridges and the dunes (p. 26): in the low polders the farmers talked to do not irrigate, while on the creek ridges a few pump from deep drains, an arable farmer about 20 mm at germination and a livestock farmer for grassland through the summer (pp. 27–28, 43). So the link runs where a farm has fresh groundwater under it. Within the year.
What farmers pump is fresh water their crops get: what pumping gains them.
When fresh water falls short, farmers irrigate with brackish ditch or well water.
Brackish water still waters the crop, so the shortfall shrinks while salt builds up.

A crop that uses less water than it needs yields less, in proportion: its relative yield falls by a crop's yield response factor times its relative shortfall in evapotranspiration, over the season 1.1 for potatoes and onions, 1.0 for sugar beet and 1.05 for winter wheat, the loss small in the vegetative and ripening periods and large in flowering and yield formation (Allen et al., 1998, FAO-56 ch. 8, eq. 90 and Table 24, after FAO paper 33, general). On the island, farmers in the western low polders find the shortfall falls mostly at germination, and a crop that emerged well loses little to drought later in the summer (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 27); a potato grower at Nieuwerkerk lost a fifth of his 2026 harvest, the potatoes smaller too, when growth stopped in the June heat and the rain came too late, his ditch water too saline to irrigate from (van Essen, 2026). Within the season.
The saltier the root zone, the more fresh water farmers use to wash the salt down.
Fresh water washes salt below the roots, for now.
The water for flushing is pumped from the lens.
A farm pays for its own pumping, part of its costs.
A supply route carries fresh water to the island.

Dry summers lower river discharge, so less river water is left to supply: a route can only carry what summer discharge and the national distribution in drought (the verdringingsreeks, IenW and Rijkswaterstaat) leave for the region, outside the CLD's scale.
connections.simplification: Folds Fresh water available for supply in drought: dry summers leave less river water for a supply route, and the route carries what is left. The sign is the product of the two steps (−, then +). Hotter, drier summers is a Constant, so no loop runs through the link. What it leaves out: the river water left for the region in drought, which the national distribution decides outside the CLD's scale, is no variable of its own.

connections.description: Farmers short of water, through their organisations, ask for a supply route, and the deciding body weighs it.
A soil with good structure carries machinery sooner after rain.
Deeper ditch levels dry the topsoil sooner in spring.
Fields that can be worked in time are planted and harvested in time.
Where fields stay too wet to work, farmers ask for lower ditch levels: what deep drainage gains them.
Low water tables expose peat to oxygen and let clay shrink and settle.

Lower ditch levels lower the counter-pressure on the salt groundwater, so the seepage pressure rises; a higher level lowers it (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 37, the board's analysis for Duiveland's water level plan). The seepage is driven by the higher water pressure in the sand below the polders' clay (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10). Within the year: the water pressures in the top layer change constantly with recharge and drainage (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3675).
Deeper drainage carries more winter rain off to the sea.

A water level plan sets the levels the board pursues and maintains (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021d, 2022), after its procedure: the executive board adopts a draft, open to views for six weeks; the general board adopts the plan; appeal is open for six weeks (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 17–18), for Duiveland from February to August 2021 (2021a, p. 53; 2021d). Its levels take effect once the works they need are in place (2025, p. 18): Duiveland's plan proposed studying a raise in 14 level areas, most possible only once the discharge capacity is enlarged (2021a, p. 69), and the works for that were still being put to the island in March 2026 (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026a). Years, so a delay.

The water board weighs farmers' need for low levels against raising them: it matches its levels to the land's use, arable land drained deeper than grassland (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 5, 7), involves farming among the interest groups as it prepares a plan and weighs their input (p. 17), and on Duiveland moves to the higher summer level in March and April as the farmers' soil work allows (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 66). How much the farmers' views weigh against the board's other aims, no source read shows: on Duiveland four views against a raise the plan proposed to study did not change the plan (p. 53). Within the year, as the plan is prepared.
Seepage and the salt it brings give the water board a reason to raise the levels.
Subsidence gives the water board a reason to raise the levels.
Rising pumping costs give the water board a reason to raise the levels.

By the water board's rules, the views sent on a draft plan within six weeks are answered in the decision, anyone affected may appeal at the court for six weeks after it, and the board consults the region first so that as few conflicts as possible arise to slow or interrupt the procedure (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 17–18). So objections can delay, change or stop a plan to raise the levels while it is pending; with none pending they change nothing, and they never lower a level. On the island the views on the two plans of 2021 changed neither: Duiveland's 25 views from six people (2021a, p. 53) and Schouwen's 11 from five, which added some studies (2021b, pp. 7–8). The only views against a raise, four on Duiveland's proposed study of one, gave as their reason the concern that flooding becomes likelier in extreme rain, not the land's value (2021a, p. 53); none of Schouwen's opposed the raises in its ten level areas (2021b, pp. 7–8, 53). The region's reactions before each draft were taken into the work on it (2021a, pp. 52–53; 2021b, p. 7). Whether anyone appealed either plan, no source read shows. Within the year, as the plan is decided.
The deeper the board drains, the more water its pumping stations lift.
Seepage water has to be pumped out too.
Winter rain drained away is pumped out of the polder.
The lower the land lies, the higher the board must lift its water.
The board passes its pumping costs on through its levy.
The levy is part of a farm's costs.

Once a crop's root zone salinity, as the conductivity of the saturated soil extract (ECe), passes its threshold, its yield falls in proportion to the excess (Allen et al., 1998, ch. 8, eq. 89): onions lose 16% per dS/m above 1.2 dS/m and potatoes 12% above 1.7, rated sensitive and moderately sensitive, against 5.9% above 7.0 for sugar beet and 7.1% above 6.0 for wheat (Table 23), so on the island's rotations salt takes most from potatoes and onions. The harm is osmotic at once and comes from sodium or chloride building up in the leaves more slowly (Munns & Tester, 2008). Table 23 is a guideline from experiments mostly under irrigation, tolerance varying with climate, soil and practice, and crops are often less tolerant as they germinate (Table 23, note 1): crop physiology that holds on the island's fields, its thresholds not measured there. Within the season.
Harvest lost to salt is income lost.

A field moved from a current crop to a new salt-tolerant one no longer has a conventional harvest for salt to take: the link holds by what Harvest lost to salt counts, the fields still under the current crops. Within the year, from the next season's crop.
connections.simplification: The new crops are taken to lose nothing to salt. That holds for crops grown on saline land, such as sea fennel and sea banana on an arable farm at Colijnsplaat (EU CAP Network, 2023), and for quinoa, among the crops better suited to saline conditions (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 63). A new crop as sensitive as the current ones loses about as much, and R4 does not run through it.

connections.description: A salt-tolerant variety loses less of its harvest to salt.
A field moved to a new crop gives up the current crop's margin.
A tolerant variety may yield or sell for less than the variety it replaces, on fresh land most.
Margin given up is income given up.
Higher prices for the current crops raise the income from carrying on.
As harvests get worse, farmers find storing water more worthwhile, and those who can pay for it store more.
connections.simplification: Folds Relative attractiveness of storing water, which gathered the drivers of this decision: each driver now points at Freshwater storage measures itself, whose description says how farmers weigh storing against their other ways through a dry summer. The attractiveness raised the decision (+), so the link keeps the sign of the step into it and no loop through it changes; the attractiveness was no actor's decision of its own. What it leaves out: whether farmers want to store, apart from whether they can (Farmers' capacity to invest), is no variable on the drawing, only in the description.

connections.description: Water stored now pays back over years, which suits a farm with a successor.
connections.simplification: Folds Relative attractiveness of storing water, which gathered the drivers of this decision: each driver now points at Freshwater storage measures itself, whose description says how farmers weigh storing against their other ways through a dry summer. The attractiveness raised the decision (+), so the link keeps the sign of the step into it and no loop through it changes; the attractiveness was no actor's decision of its own. What it leaves out: whether farmers want to store, apart from whether they can (Farmers' capacity to invest), is no variable on the drawing, only in the description.

connections.description: What a storage measure costs comes out of the money left to invest.
The saltier the field, the more a tolerant variety is worth against the current one, so the more farmers grow it, perhaps only past a threshold.
connections.simplification: Folds Relative attractiveness of salt-tolerant varieties, which gathered the drivers of this decision: each driver now points at Adoption of salt-tolerant varieties itself, whose description says that farmers weigh a tolerant variety against the one they grow now. The attractiveness raised the decision (+), so the link keeps the sign of the step into it and no loop through it changes; the attractiveness was no actor's decision of its own.

connections.description: Better tolerant varieties on the market make switching more worthwhile, so more farmers grow them.
connections.simplification: Folds Relative attractiveness of salt-tolerant varieties, which gathered the drivers of this decision: each driver now points at Adoption of salt-tolerant varieties itself, whose description says that farmers weigh a tolerant variety against the one they grow now. The attractiveness raised the decision (+), so the link keeps the sign of the step into it and no loop through it changes; the attractiveness was no actor's decision of its own.

connections.description: The saltier the field, the more a new salt-tolerant crop is worth against the current crops, so the more farmers grow it, perhaps only past a threshold.
connections.simplification: Folds Relative attractiveness of new salt-tolerant crops, which gathered the drivers of this decision: each driver now points at Adoption of new salt-tolerant crops itself, whose description says that farmers weigh a new crop against their current crops. The attractiveness raised the decision (+), so the link keeps the sign of the step into it and no loop through it changes; the attractiveness was no actor's decision of its own. What it leaves out: whether farmers want to switch, apart from whether they can (Farmers' capacity to invest), is no variable on the drawing, only in the description.

connections.simplification: Folds Relative attractiveness of new salt-tolerant crops, which gathered the drivers of this decision: each driver now points at Adoption of new salt-tolerant crops itself, whose description says that farmers weigh a new crop against their current crops. The attractiveness raised the decision (+), so the link keeps the sign of the step into it and no loop through it changes; the attractiveness was no actor's decision of its own. What it leaves out: whether farmers want to switch, apart from whether they can (Farmers' capacity to invest), is no variable on the drawing, only in the description.

connections.simplification: Folds Relative attractiveness of new salt-tolerant crops, which gathered the drivers of this decision: each driver now points at Adoption of new salt-tolerant crops itself, whose description says that farmers weigh a new crop against their current crops. The attractiveness raised the decision (+), so the link keeps the sign of the step into it and no loop through it changes; the attractiveness was no actor's decision of its own. What it leaves out: whether farmers want to switch, apart from whether they can (Farmers' capacity to invest), is no variable on the drawing, only in the description.

connections.description: Farmers who know how to grow and sell a new crop find it less risky, so more of them grow it.
connections.simplification: Folds Relative attractiveness of new salt-tolerant crops, which gathered the drivers of this decision: each driver now points at Adoption of new salt-tolerant crops itself, whose description says that farmers weigh a new crop against their current crops. The attractiveness raised the decision (+), so the link keeps the sign of the step into it and no loop through it changes; the attractiveness was no actor's decision of its own. What it leaves out: whether farmers want to switch, apart from whether they can (Farmers' capacity to invest), is no variable on the drawing, only in the description.

connections.description: Growing a new crop, on their own fields or their neighbours', teaches farmers how.
Switching costs (machines, the first years of a new crop) come out of the money left to invest.
More hectares of new crops on the island, more harvest to process.
Growers elsewhere add to the harvest a local plant could draw on.
More harvest within reach makes a local plant more worthwhile, so processors build or keep capacity on or near the island rather than process the crops elsewhere.
connections.simplification: Folds Attractiveness of processing new crops locally, which gathered the drivers of this decision: each driver now points at Local processing capacity for new crops itself, whose description says that buyers and processors weigh it against processing the crops elsewhere. The attractiveness raised the decision (+), so the link keeps the sign of the step into it and no loop through it changes; the attractiveness was no actor's decision of its own.

connections.description: Stable demand makes investing in processing more worthwhile.
connections.simplification: Folds Attractiveness of processing new crops locally, which gathered the drivers of this decision: each driver now points at Local processing capacity for new crops itself, whose description says that buyers and processors weigh it against processing the crops elsewhere. The attractiveness raised the decision (+), so the link keeps the sign of the step into it and no loop through it changes; the attractiveness was no actor's decision of its own.

connections.description: A plant nearby cuts transport, so farmers keep more of the price.
Processors elsewhere compete for the harvest and set the price a local plant must match.
A farm that keeps its current crops keeps investing in their machines and storage.
Growing the current crops year after year builds up know-how in growing, storing and selling them, and that know-how is of little use for a new crop.
connections.simplification: Folds Know-how of the current crops, a stock between the two: growing the current crops builds know-how, which is of little use for a new crop. The sign is the product of the two steps (+, then +), so no loop through the link changes, and know-how is no actor's decision. What one link leaves out: the know-how as a stock of its own, built up over years of growing the crops.

connections.description: The more a farm owns for its current crops, the more a switch to a new crop writes off.
What a farm would lose by switching ties it to its current crops.
Money left to invest can go to carrying on: wells, irrigation, drains, a new harvester.
A farm tied to its current crops spends on keeping them.
What it spends there is not left for other uses.
A new harvester or store adds to the capital for the current crops.
Wells and irrigation let a farm pump more.
A farm with less equity against its debt is a riskier loan.
A plan that may change what the land can earn enters a bank's risk analysis before it is decided.
Banks lend less to farms they see as riskier.
Banks charge more for loans they see as riskier.
Credit is part of what a farm can invest.
New loans add to a farm's debt against its assets.
More debt, more to pay each year.
A higher premium raises the interest farms pay.
Interest is part of a farm's costs.
A farm with high debt payments keeps its lucrative but salt-sensitive crops to meet them.
Farms that cannot refinance sell up.
Highly leveraged farms are the ones sold in a forced sale or bankruptcy.
A farm with a successor stays with the family; one without is sold when its farmer retires.
Farmers attached to their land sell it later, often only when forced.
Expropriated land passes to the public body that takes it, after a legal procedure.
Land that changes hands leaves arable farming when its next holder does not farm it.
Where arable farming still pays for a buyer or successor, the next holder keeps the land arable.

Arable land needs lower ditch levels than grassland or nature. By the water board's rules for its whole area, a water level plan starts from an optimal level for each use and soil, the farmland's derived from the optimal drain depths for farming: for arable farming and horticulture 120 cm below the surface on salt-marsh clay (schorgronden) with no sand within 1.2 m, down to 60 on peat, for permanent grassland as a rule 20 cm less (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 7, 19), and for nature 0 cm as a general starting point, its levels set with the site managers, as Duiveland's analysis applied them to its land-use map of 2018 (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 29). So the more hectares farmed as arable land, the more land whose farmers need low levels, in spring as their soil work allows (2021a, p. 66); how strongly they ask for them, no source read shows (Farmers' demand for deep polder drainage → Water board's plans to raise ditch levels). Within the year: the need goes with the land's use each season, while the land leaves arable use only as it changes hands (Arable land in the polders).
A farm that pays finds a successor more easily.
A plan to raise the ditch levels makes owners fear their land will lose value.
Farmers who trust that public bodies keep their commitments object less.
Farmers attached to their land resist plans for it beyond what it is worth in money.
Objections and appeals delay, change or stop plans for the island's water and land after public bodies announced them, and plans changed or dropped teach farmers not to count on the next one.
connections.simplification: Folds Plans changed or dropped: objections and appeals change, delay or stop plans, and the changes teach farmers not to count on the next plan. The sign is the product of the two steps (+, then −), so no loop through the link changes. The public bodies' decisions on their plans stay drawn, on the links from Objections to land-use plans into Water board's plans to raise ditch levels and Farmland planned for other uses; this link carries only what farmers learn from the changes.

connections.description: Where owners will not sell, a public body may expropriate.
Land taken by force lowers farmers' trust in government.
Objections delay, change or stop a plan in which the municipality designates farmland for another use, while it is pending; with none pending, they change nothing.
A plan that designates farmland for another use leads its owners and the farmers who work it to object, appeal and lobby against it.
Farmland the plan designates for another use leaves arable farming once the plan is carried out on it; how long that takes waits for a source.

loops.name: Salty soil takes in less rain
Land value, objections and ditch levels
Less arable land, less deep drainage
The water board raises levels against seepage
Banks lend less as leverage rises
Capital ties farms to their crops
